chapters.title: Chapter 6: Markets at Work and in Your Pocket

lessons.title: Where Your Salary Meets the Markets: ESOPs, EPF, NPS and Mutual Fund SIPs

children.text: Most employees believe they will start investing later. In reality it began with your first salary credit. Money has been flowing from your payroll into bonds and equities every month, through channels you did not choose and probably have never reviewed. This lesson maps all of them, so you know what you own.

body.text: You are not deciding whether to be invested in markets. You already are, through EPF, possibly NPS, possibly ESOPs. The only open question is whether that combination is deliberate or accidental.

body.title: A Mid-Career Employee's Actual Market Exposure (Illustrative)

body.label: The Concentration Nobody Plans
body.context: Your salary, your ESOPs and often your annual bonus all depend on the same employer. If that company struggles, your income, your savings and your job security are hit at the same moment, by the same event.

body.text: This is the single largest financial risk most salaried professionals carry, and it is almost never on anyone's radar. Diversification is not a sophisticated investing concept here; it is the basic observation that your rent should not depend on one company's quarterly results twice over.

children.text: ESOPs, From Grant to Cash

markDefs.definition: The process by which granted options become exercisable over time, often with a one-year cliff followed by graded vesting across subsequent years.
The fixed price at which a vested option allows you to buy a share, set at the time of grant. Also called the strike price.
The act of paying the exercise price to convert vested options into actual shares. This is usually the point at which a tax event arises for the employee.

children.text: An option is a right to buy your employer's shares at a fixed
exercise price
, once it has cleared
vesting
. Nothing is yours until it vests, and even then nothing happens until you
exercise
by paying that price. Restricted stock units work slightly differently, since they convert into shares on vesting without a purchase price, but the sequence below is otherwise the same.

body.title: The Four Stages of an ESOP

events.title: Grant
events.description: You are awarded a number of options at a stated exercise price. Nothing is owned, nothing is taxed, and nothing can be sold. A grant is a promise with conditions attached.

events.title: Vesting
events.description: Options become exercisable according to the schedule, commonly after a one-year cliff and then in instalments. Leaving before a vesting date usually forfeits whatever has not yet vested.

events.title: Exercise
events.description: You pay the exercise price and receive shares. The difference between the value of the share at that moment and the price you paid is treated as a benefit from employment, and tax is generally deducted through payroll at this point.

events.title: Sale
events.description: When you eventually sell, any further gain above the value used at exercise is treated as a capital gain, with the treatment depending on how long you held the shares and whether they are listed.

body.latex: \text{Benefit at Exercise} = (\text{Share Value at Exercise} - \text{Exercise Price}) \times \text{Number of Options}
body.caption: This first slice is taxed as employment income. Any gain after exercise is a separate, later capital gain.

stats.label: Options Exercised
stats.context: At an exercise price of ₹100 each

stats.label: Benefit at Exercise
stats.context: Share valued at ₹400, so (₹400 − ₹100) × 1,000, taxed as employment income

stats.label: Later Capital Gain
stats.context: If sold at ₹550, the gain above the ₹400 exercise value

body.text: Notice the cash flow. At exercise you pay ₹1,00,000 and also owe tax on a ₹3,00,000 benefit, usually deducted from your salary that month, while holding shares you may not be able to sell immediately. Employees at unlisted companies have been caught badly by this, paying real tax on a paper gain in a share with no market. Before exercising, confirm three things: the cash required, the tax that will be withheld, and whether you can actually sell.

body.title: Work Out the Taxable Benefit
body.prompt: You exercise 800 vested options with an exercise price of ₹50 each, when the share is valued at ₹300. What is the benefit treated as employment income, in ₹?
body.explanation: (₹300 − ₹50) × 800 = ₹2,00,000. That amount is added to your income for the year and tax is generally deducted through payroll, regardless of whether you sell a single share. Plan for both the ₹40,000 exercise cost and the tax outflow in the same month.

body.title: What to Read in Your Own Grant Letter

children.text: Six clauses decide what your ESOPs are actually worth to you:
The vesting schedule.
How much vests, when, and whether there is a cliff. This determines what you would leave behind if you resigned next month.
The exercise window after leaving.
Many plans give departing employees a short period to exercise vested options, sometimes only weeks. Miss it and vested options lapse, which is one of the most common ways employees lose real money.
Whether cashless exercise is allowed.
Some plans let you sell enough shares simultaneously to cover the exercise price and tax, which solves the cash flow problem entirely. Others require you to fund it yourself.
How the share is valued if unlisted.
For an unlisted company, valuation comes from a prescribed process rather than a market price, and that number drives your tax.
Clawback and bad leaver clauses.
Conditions under which the company can cancel or reclaim your options, including how resignation, termination and joining a competitor are treated.
Liquidity provisions.
For unlisted companies, whether there is any buyback or secondary sale mechanism at all. Without one, vested options may have no route to cash for years.
EPF and NPS: The Two You Rarely Look At

columns.label: Employees' Provident Fund
points: Statutory for covered employees, with an employer contribution alongside yours
Predominantly debt, with a limited portion routed into equity index funds
Returns are declared by the EPFO rather than varying daily
Access is largely at retirement, with specified exceptions
Simple and low-effort, but the allocation is not yours to set

columns.label: National Pension System
points: Voluntary, or offered as a corporate benefit through your employer
You choose the mix across equity, corporate debt, government securities and alternatives, within regulatory caps
Value moves with markets daily, like a mutual fund
Largely locked until 60, with limited partial withdrawals permitted
Lower cost than most alternatives, but requires you to make choices

body.text: Two things are worth knowing about NPS specifically. Regulations cap how much of your NPS corpus can sit in equity, and the default lifecycle option reduces equity automatically as you age. If you never made an active choice, you are in the default, and that is a decision by omission rather than an absence of decision.

body.text: Deliberately, this table states no rates, thresholds or section references. Indian tax law on capital gains, provident fund interest and retirement withdrawals has changed repeatedly in recent years, and a new consolidated income tax statute has replaced the earlier one. Any figure quoted here would risk being wrong for the year in which you read it. Confirm current rates, limits and section references with a qualified tax professional or the income tax department's own material before acting on anything in this lesson.

body.title: Sixty Percent in One Company
body.scenario: You are a senior manager at a listed Indian company, twelve years into your career. Your salary and annual bonus come from this employer. Vested ESOPs and shares from earlier exercises now make up about 60% of everything you have saved. Your EPF corpus is most of the rest, and you have a small SIP. A colleague tells you to hold the shares because the company is doing well and the stock has trebled since you joined.
body.prompt: How should you think about this? Set out a framework rather than a verdict.
body.modelAnswer: Start by naming the risk accurately, because it is not really an investing question. Your salary, your bonus, your job security and 60% of your savings all depend on the same company, which means a single bad outcome at one employer hits your income and your accumulated wealth simultaneously. That is concentration on top of concentration, and it would be flagged immediately if any investment manager presented it as a portfolio. Note that your colleague's argument, that the stock has trebled and the company is doing well, is an argument about past performance and present sentiment, not about the risk you are carrying. Both of those can be true while the concentration remains unwise. A sensible framework has four steps. First, quantify: write down what percentage of your total savings sits in employer stock, and separately how many months of expenses you could cover if both your salary and that stock disappeared in the same quarter. Second, decide a target, in advance and in writing, for what share of your savings you are comfortable holding in your employer, since a rule set calmly is far easier to follow than a decision made during a price move. Third, if reducing, do it gradually and mechanically rather than trying to pick a moment, and route the proceeds into something genuinely uncorrelated with your employer's fortunes, which usually means diversified funds rather than another stock in the same sector. Fourth, plan the practicalities before acting: check your trading window and insider trading obligations from the previous lesson, check whether you hold any UPSI, understand the tax consequences of a sale in the year you make it, and get proper advice on the tax before rather than after. What this lesson cannot tell you is whether to sell, how much, or when. That depends on your goals, your family's circumstances, your other assets and your tax position, and it is exactly the sort of decision worth paying a SEBI-registered investment adviser for. The narrow point here is that leaving the allocation unexamined because it happened by default is itself a choice, and usually the least considered one available.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The process by which granted stock options gradually become exercisable over time is called ___.
body.explanation: Vesting is what converts a promise into something you can act on. Options that have not vested are generally forfeited if you leave, which is why the vesting schedule is the first thing to read in any grant letter.

body.title: A One-Hour Audit of Your Payroll Investments
steps: Download your EPF passbook and note the balance and how it has grown, since most people have never looked
Check whether your employer offers corporate NPS, and if you are enrolled, find out which allocation option you are in
List your ESOP grants: how many options, at what exercise price, vested and unvested, and the exercise window if you were to leave
Add up what percentage of your total savings depends on your employer, counting shares, vested options and any company-linked plan
Check your SIPs to see what you actually own, including whether two funds hold largely the same companies
Confirm nominations are current on EPF, NPS, demat and mutual fund accounts, which takes minutes and is routinely neglected
Write down one number: how many months of expenses you could fund if your salary stopped and your employer's share price halved in the same quarter

body.label: EPFO Member Portal
body.description: Check your EPF passbook, balance and employer contribution history. Worth doing annually, since missing employer deposits are easier to fix when caught early than years later.

points: Your salary already flows into markets through EPF, possibly NPS and possibly ESOPs, whether or not you ever made an investment decision
EPF is mostly debt with a limited equity portion and an allocation you do not control, while NPS lets you choose within regulatory caps
If you never made an active NPS choice, you are in the default lifecycle option, which is a decision by omission
ESOPs move through grant, vesting, exercise and sale, and only vesting and exercise are within your control
Exercise creates a tax event on the benefit even if you cannot sell the shares, so confirm the cash needed, the tax withheld and your ability to sell first
The exercise window after leaving a company is short in many plans, and missing it is a common way employees lose vested value
The biggest financial risk most employees carry is concentration: salary, bonus, job and savings all depending on one company
Tax rules on all of these have changed repeatedly, so verify current rates and limits rather than relying on what was true last year

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment, tax or legal advice, and nothing here is a recommendation about your employer's shares or any investment. ESOP terms differ from company to company and are governed by your own plan documents. Contribution rates, caps, withdrawal rules and tax treatment for EPF, NPS and market-linked investments are set by statute and regulation and change over time. All figures used are illustrative. Consult your plan documents, your compliance team and a qualified tax or investment professional before acting.
